I have a daughter and only had post-partum depression symptoms for one week (I wasn't sleeping), and my rituals and anxieties are under control. I don't think there would be any way for me to be a good mom without being on Prozac. My anxiety would be crippling again and would prevent me from being a present, level-headed mother. I had gone off the meds for two weeks a year ago (prescription was unavailable), and while it wasn't great (anxiety and rituals returned), it wasn't anything like portrayals of coming off of heroin. comments.text: SSRI withdrawal is a problem literally caused by the pharmaceutical industry.  They generally don’t want people to discontinue medications, so they make it difficult by only producing specific doses and making the pills smaller and harder to accurately split and measure into smaller doses.  Compounding pharmacies can help with liquid formulations and tapering, but not everyone will be able to access to that.  I ended up essentially making my own “liquid citalopram” and tapering off super slowly over 3 months.  I initially tried the two week taper recommended by my provider, and it did not go very well.

comments.text: I’ve been on SSRI’s for about six years now, and I’ll likely need to be on them for the rest of my life. I was 12 when I was diagnosed by a therapist with depression/anxiety and 18 when I officially diagnosed with severe depression and severe anxiety. My entire life has changed. I went from not being able to get up in the morning if my anxiety didn’t kick into high gear to waking up and getting out of bed with more ease than I knew was possible. I didn’t know people could wake up and not want to immediately cry. I function close to a neurotypical person because of my SSRI’s. My mom and my grandma are on the same medication and we have all needed to stay on it for life. For me, withdrawal isn’t bad. What is bad is the depression and anxiety that comes back with a force. My withdrawal is a headache, my function is close to none. I know people who have known me before and after being on medication and they all have told me how different I have been since being on them. And here’s the kicker, I did everything I was supposed to. I ate right, I exercised all the time, I had a regular and good sleep schedule, I drank enough water, I had close friends, and I saw a therapist. None of it cured me. I was determined to beat the depression that was a part of me without medication, but after 7 years of trying to beat it, I realized via my psych professors that my brain literally was functioning differently. SSRI’s are used to actually change how your neurons accept information and chemicals. I had a physical problem and this medication solved the problem. I function now. If I had to go off of them, I’d be the person I was before and that person was so miserable and in mental “pain” she nearly missed out on the next 6 years of her life. Can medication be over prescribed? Yes. Is depression sometimes temporary? Yes. However, are depression and anxiety also very genetic and can require consistent medication to work properly (like insulin)? YES! These stories often frustrate me because depression and anxiety often treated as just a temporary emotion like happiness or sadness. It often isn’t. Worrying that your friend is mad at you because they woke up in a bad mood is not normal. Worrying that your coworker is mad at you because in the two seconds you said hi to them they said hi back weirdly. Feeling like crying after waking up every morning is not normal. Medication for mental health issues is often treating a physical imbalance that isn’t easily seen, but can still do a lot of damage. I just hope that people see the real human beings that will be harmed if access to these medications are taken away or are limited further.
comments.author: @MrsGeekyFreakyNerd
